16440: A turnabout is a complete reversal — a full 180-degree change from one direction, position, or state to another. Picture someone walking down a path, then spinning around and walking back the way they came. That simple physical image of turning all the way around is the beating heart of every meaning this word has.
The Most Common Meaning: A Complete Change or Reversal

In everyday and journalistic language, a turnabout refers to a dramatic, often sudden shift in opinion, behavior, policy, or fortune. Crucially, it isn't a small tweak or minor adjustment — it is a complete change from one position to the opposite.

A politician who spent years loudly opposing a law and then announces they now fully support it has made a turnabout in their position. A sports team that was losing every game and then starts winning the championship is said to have staged a remarkable turnabout. A company on the edge of bankruptcy that becomes highly profitable has achieved a financial turnabout.

Notice the pattern: the change is total, and it is almost always surprising or dramatic. A gentle shift in opinion does not earn this word. A turnabout is the kind of change that makes people raise their eyebrows.

Perhaps the single most important thing to know about this word is the phrase "turnabout is fair play." You will encounter it often, and it captures a slightly distinct shade of the word's meaning.

In this sense, a turnabout refers to the act of reversing the roles between two people or parties — specifically, doing to someone the very same thing they did to you.

The phrase as a whole means: if someone treats you a certain way, it is only fair that you get to treat them the same way in return.

Here is a simple example. Imagine your friend constantly teases you about your cooking. One day you discover that their cooking is just as bad, and you tease them right back. You could smile and say, "Turnabout is fair play!" The roles have been flipped. The person who was always the target is now the one doing the teasing. The phrase carries no deep moral complexity — it simply asserts that you started it, so I am entitled to respond in kind.

The word also has two concrete, real-world meanings that are less abstract.

First, a turnabout can refer to a physical space — such as a wide area at the end of a private road or driveway — that is specifically designed so a vehicle can turn around without having to reverse awkwardly for a long distance. It is simply a place built for the purpose of changing direction.

Second, in older and now less common usage, a turnabout can refer to a merry-go-round — a rotating platform of the kind found at playgrounds or fairgrounds. The connection is transparent: it literally turns around and around continuously.
The School Dance Meaning (A Cultural Note for American English)

In parts of the United States, a Turnabout — often written with a capital T — is a type of school dance where the usual social roles are reversed: girls invite boys, rather than the other way around. It is sometimes also called a "Sadie Hawkins dance." The logic is the same reversal principle: the traditional arrangement is flipped on its head. If you ever read about this in an American novel or TV show set in a high school, now you will know exactly what it means.
How and When This Word Is Used

Turnabout belongs more to formal writing, journalism, and public discourse than to casual everyday conversation. You are far more likely to read it in a news article — "the brand's stunning turnabout surprised analysts" — than to hear a friend drop it naturally into a chat.

In terms of tone, it tends to be neutral to subtly positive when describing a recovery or comeback (a struggling organization stages a turnabout). In political contexts, however, it can carry a gently critical edge, hinting that someone has abandoned a long-held principle. As with most words, the surrounding context tells you which flavor is intended.

To sum it all up: a turnabout is always about reversal — whether that is a reversal of opinion, performance, fortune, roles between people, or simply the direction of a vehicle on a road. The degree of reversal is always complete, never partial. That one unifying idea — turning all the way around — ties every meaning of this word together.
16441: "Turnaround" captures the image of something literally turning around — going in one direction, then reversing completely. Every meaning of this word flows from that central idea of a full reversal or a full cycle of completion.
Meaning 1: A Complete Reversal of a Situation

This is the most common and most important meaning. A turnaround is when a situation changes dramatically from one state to its opposite — most often from bad to good.

Think of a company that has been losing money for three years. Then a new CEO joins, makes bold changes, and suddenly the company starts making profits. That dramatic change is called a turnaround.

Examples:

  • "The football team had lost eight games in a row, but their new coach led an incredible turnaround — they won the championship that year."
  • "Her health turnaround surprised everyone. Six months ago she could barely walk; now she runs marathons."
  • "The country's economic turnaround began after the government reformed its tax policies."

Important nuances:

  • A turnaround usually implies the change is significant and noteworthy — not just a slight improvement, but a real reversal of direction.
  • While it most commonly means going from bad to good, it can technically describe a shift in either direction. However, you'd rarely call a worsening situation a "turnaround" without adding a word like "negative" or "unfortunate" turnaround.
  • In business, a turnaround often refers specifically to the rescue and recovery of a failing company. Business people even talk about a "turnaround specialist" — someone hired specifically to fix struggling companies.
Meaning 2: The Time Taken to Complete a Task and Return the Result

A turnaround (or more commonly, turnaround time) refers to how long it takes to finish a piece of work and deliver it back to whoever requested it. Think of it as the round-trip time of a job: you send a task, it gets done, and it comes back to you.

Examples:

  • "What's the turnaround on these blood test results?" — meaning: how long will it take to get the results back?
  • "Our printing shop has a 48-hour turnaround." — meaning: you'll have your printed materials back within 48 hours of placing the order.
  • "The editor promised a quick turnaround on the manuscript." — meaning: she would review and return it soon.
  • "The turnaround for visa applications is currently six weeks." — meaning: you'll wait six weeks to get a decision.

Why this connects to the core idea: Imagine handing a package to someone, they process it, and then it comes back to you — it has "turned around" and come back. The turnaround time is how long that round trip takes.

This meaning is extremely common in professional and everyday settings — publishing, healthcare, logistics, customer service, printing, manufacturing, and many more. Whenever someone asks "how long will this take?", the answer is often expressed as a turnaround time.
Meaning 3: The Process of Preparing a Vehicle for Its Next Journey

In transportation — particularly in aviation, but also shipping and trucking — a turnaround refers to the complete cycle of a vehicle arriving at a stop, being unloaded, cleaned, refueled, reloaded, and made ready to depart again.

Examples:

  • "The airline is famous for its fast turnarounds — its planes are rarely on the ground for more than 30 minutes."
  • "A slow turnaround at the port cost the shipping company thousands of dollars."
  • "Ground crew efficiency is key to a smooth turnaround."

Why this matters: Airlines, shipping companies, and transport businesses make money when their vehicles are moving, not sitting idle. The faster the turnaround, the more journeys a vehicle can complete in a day, and the more money the company earns. This is why turnaround time is watched very closely in these industries.
Meaning 4: A Physical Space for Vehicles to Reverse Direction

Less common but worth knowing: a turnaround can refer to a physical area — usually at the end of a dead-end road or driveway — where a vehicle can turn around and go back the way it came.

Examples:

  • "The delivery driver couldn't back out of the narrow lane, so we built a turnaround at the end."
  • "There's a small turnaround at the top of the hill where buses can reverse."

This meaning is the most literal of all — the vehicle actually turns around in that space.

Notice that every meaning involves some form of completing a cycle or reversing direction:

  • In meaning 1, a situation reverses its course — from failure to success.
  • In meaning 2, work goes out and comes back — the round-trip time of a job.
  • In meaning 3, a vehicle arrives, gets processed, and leaves again — a complete service cycle.
  • In meaning 4, a vehicle literally turns around in a physical space.

These are the most natural word combinations you'll encounter with "turnaround":

  • turnaround time — the time taken to complete and return a task (Meaning 2)
  • quick turnaround / fast turnaround — completing something rapidly
  • remarkable / stunning / incredible turnaround — a dramatic reversal of fortunes (Meaning 1)
  • economic turnaround — a country or region recovering from recession
  • turnaround plan / turnaround strategy — a plan to rescue a failing business
  • complete turnaround — a total, 180-degree reversal ("He made a complete turnaround in his views on climate change.")
One Word, Tested in Different Sentences

To make sure you can recognize "turnaround" in any context, read these and notice which meaning applies:

  1. "The new manager engineered a remarkable turnaround for the struggling restaurant." → Meaning 1 (situation reversed from bad to good)
  2. "Our standard turnaround for custom orders is five business days." → Meaning 2 (time to complete and return a job)
  3. "The aircraft's turnaround at Delhi airport took just 40 minutes." → Meaning 3 (vehicle serviced and readied to depart)
  4. "They widened the driveway and added a turnaround at the end." → Meaning 4 (physical space)

If you had to remember just one thing: "turnaround" is about reversing direction or completing a cycle. When something bad becomes good — that's a turnaround. When a job goes out and comes back — that's a turnaround. When a vehicle arrives, gets serviced, and departs — that's a turnaround. The word always implies that something has gone full circle or completely changed course.
16442: A turncoat is a person who abandons the group, side, or cause they once belonged to — and then joins or supports the opposing side. The switch is seen as a betrayal, and the word is always used with a negative, condemning tone. Nobody proudly calls themselves a turncoat.
The Key Idea: It's Not Just Changing Your Mind

This is the most important thing to understand. A turncoat doesn't just quietly change their opinion. They make an active switch — from one side to the other — in a way that hurts or betrays the people they used to stand with.

Think of it like being on a team, quitting that team, and then going to play against them. That's the spirit of the word.

The word appears most often in the context of politics, war, business, and loyalty. Here are some clear real-world examples to make it concrete:

A politician who has spent years in one party, publicly defending its values, and then suddenly switches to the rival party — especially if they start attacking their former colleagues — would be called a turncoat by those they left behind.

A soldier who fights for one army, then defects and starts fighting for the enemy is a classic turncoat.

A senior employee who leaves a company, takes its trade secrets, and joins a direct competitor to help defeat the company they came from — people would call that person a turncoat.
What Makes Someone a Turncoat (and What Doesn't)

Not every change of opinion or group makes someone a turncoat. Three things usually need to be true:

First, the person must have once had a clear, known loyalty — they were genuinely "on a side."

Second, they must switch to the opposing side, not just walk away neutrally.

Third, the switch is seen as a betrayal — meaning the people left behind feel hurt, used, or endangered by it. Often, the turncoat actively works against their former group after switching.

If someone simply changes their personal opinion in private, or quietly leaves a group without joining the opposition, most people wouldn't call them a turncoat. The betrayal and the active switch are what define the word.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

"Turncoat" is a strongly negative, accusatory word. When someone calls another person a turncoat, they are expressing anger, disgust, and a sense of being stabbed in the back. It suggests that the person switched sides out of self-interest, cowardice, or opportunism — not because of any genuine or honest change of heart.

Even if a person switched sides for what they believe are good reasons, the people they left behind will use this word to shame and discredit them.
Synonyms That Are Close in Meaning

Several words carry a similar meaning, each with a slightly different shade:

Traitor is the broadest and harshest — it means someone who betrays their country, group, or trust. All turncoats could be called traitors, but "traitor" is wider and more serious in tone.

Defector is more neutral and factual — it's often used in political or military contexts (e.g., a spy who defects to another country). It describes the act of switching sides without necessarily carrying as much emotional condemnation as "turncoat."

Renegade refers to a person who deserts and rejects the principles of a group. It overlaps with turncoat but can also refer to someone who simply rebels and goes their own way, not necessarily joining the other side.

Double-crosser focuses specifically on betraying someone who trusted you — often after making a deal or agreement.

Among all of these, turncoat is particularly vivid because it emphasizes the switching of sides and the feeling of seeing someone who used to face the same direction as you suddenly turn and face against you.

"When the general surrendered his own army's battle plans to the enemy, his soldiers called him a turncoat and never forgave him."

"She had campaigned hard for the party for fifteen years, so when she crossed the aisle and endorsed the opposition, the press immediately branded her a turncoat."

"He thought he was making a brave, principled decision — but to everyone around him, he looked like nothing more than a turncoat."
One-Line Summary to Remember It By
A turncoat is someone who betrays their own side by switching to the enemy — and is condemned for it.
16443:
A turnkey is something — a product, a property, a business, or a system — that is completely finished and fully ready to use the moment it is handed over, with no additional work required from the person receiving it.

The name captures this idea well: everything is already done for you, and all you have to do is "turn the key" — like turning a key to start a car, or turning a key to open the door of a brand-new home. The instant you turn it, everything works.

The defining characteristic is that it is delivered in a finished, operational state. The provider has handled everything — the planning, the building, the setup, the testing — and the buyer inherits a complete, working thing.

This is the opposite of receiving something in an incomplete or raw state, where the buyer still has to do significant work before it's usable.

Real estate
A turnkey property (or simply "a turnkey") is a home that has been fully renovated — fresh paint, new flooring, repaired fixtures, working appliances — so the buyer can move in on the same day they purchase it. There's nothing to fix, nothing to upgrade. It's ready.

Compare this to buying a fixer-upper, where you spend months and significant money making the home livable before you can actually live in it. A fixer-upper is the opposite of a turnkey.

Business
A turnkey business is one that is already running — with employees hired, systems in place, customers established, and money coming in. The new owner simply steps in and takes over. There's no building from scratch.

Franchises are a classic example. When you buy a McDonald's franchise, the franchisor gives you the brand, the recipes, the equipment specifications, the training system, the supplier relationships, and the operational playbook. You receive a business that's ready to open. That's a turnkey.

Construction
In a turnkey contract, a construction company takes full responsibility for a building project — everything from the initial design to the final coat of paint — and hands the client a completed, move-in-ready structure at the end. The client doesn't have to manage architects, contractors, suppliers, or permits. They just receive the finished building.

Technology
A turnkey system is software or hardware that arrives pre-installed, pre-configured, and tested. The user doesn't have to set anything up. They just plug it in (or log in) and start working.
A Concrete Example to Make It Click

Suppose you want to open a coffee shop.

Option A (not a turnkey): You rent an empty commercial space. You then separately hire a designer, purchase espresso machines, build counters, install plumbing, source coffee beans, hire and train staff, set up a point-of-sale system, get the required permits, and build a website. After months of effort and coordination, the shop is finally ready to open.

Option B (a turnkey): You buy a package where someone hands you a fully equipped coffee shop — machines installed, counters built, staff trained, permits secured, POS system running, supplier agreements in place. On Day 1, you just show up, turn the key, and open the doors to customers.

Option B is a turnkey. All the complex, time-consuming work has already been done by someone else. Your involvement begins only at the finish line.

When something is called a turnkey, it signals:

  • Zero setup effort on the buyer's part
  • Complete delivery — nothing is missing or unfinished
  • Immediate usability — it works from the moment of handover
  • The provider bears all the complexity — the buyer doesn't need expertise, tools, or extra resources to get started

This is why turnkeys are attractive. They save time, reduce risk, and eliminate the need for the buyer to become an expert in something outside their core focus. A business owner who wants a coffee shop doesn't necessarily want to become an expert in construction, plumbing, and equipment installation. A turnkey spares them all of that.
An Important Nuance: Turnkey as a Selling Point

"Turnkey" is frequently used as a marketing and sales term. When a property, business, or system is advertised as a "turnkey," the seller is essentially promising: this is hassle-free and ready to go.

In practice, this means buyers should still do their homework. Not every seller's definition of "ready to use" meets the same standard. Some sellers loosely call something a turnkey when it still has gaps or hidden problems. So while the word signals completeness and readiness, a careful buyer will verify what exactly is included — and in what condition.

The word is a promise. Whether the promise holds depends on the specific deal.

In older English, a turnkey referred to a jailer — a prison guard whose specific job was to literally turn the large iron keys that locked and unlocked prison cell doors. This was a real occupational title in the 18th and 19th centuries.

This meaning is essentially obsolete today. You're very unlikely to encounter it in any modern text. In virtually every modern context — in business, real estate, technology, and construction — "turnkey" means the complete-and-ready-to-use concept described above.

A turnkey is something completely built, set up, and ready for immediate use, requiring nothing further from the recipient. The provider does all the work; the buyer just starts. It's the idea of maximum completeness and minimum friction — everything done, delivered, and functional, right from the first moment.
16444: The word turnoff has two distinct meanings — one literal and one figurative. Both are common in everyday English.
Meaning 1: A place where you exit a main road

A turnoff is a spot on a road where you leave the main path and take a smaller road, a side road, or an exit that branches off in a different direction.

Think of it like this: you are driving on a big highway, and there is a point where a smaller road splits away from it, leading you toward a town, a destination, or a different route. That splitting point — the place where you "turn off" the main road — is called a turnoff.

Examples:

  • "The turnoff for the beach is about five kilometers ahead — don't miss it."
  • "He almost passed the turnoff because it had no sign."
  • "Take the second turnoff after the bridge."

The key idea here is leaving a larger road to enter a smaller one. The turnoff is not the entire smaller road — it is specifically the point of departure, the place where the two roads diverge and you choose to exit.

You will hear this word most often in driving directions and road navigation.
Meaning 2: Something that kills your interest, attraction, or enthusiasm

This is the more widely used meaning in casual conversation. A turnoff is anything — a behavior, a quality, a habit, a sight, a smell, a situation — that makes you suddenly lose interest, feel repelled, or become less attracted to something or someone.

The logic of the word is simple: imagine your interest or enthusiasm as something that is "turned on" (like a switch). A turnoff switches it off. It kills the positive feeling you had.

Examples:

  • "He seemed attractive at first, but his constant bragging was a huge turnoff."
  • "The restaurant looked beautiful, but the smell near the kitchen was a real turnoff."
  • "For many voters, the candidate's aggressive tone was a turnoff."
  • "Rudeness is an instant turnoff for her — she simply walks away."

This meaning applies across many situations:

  • Romantic/personal attraction — This is where the word is most commonly used. A turnoff is something that makes a person less romantically or physically attracted to someone else. It is the opposite of a turn-on (something that increases attraction or interest).
    • "She finds overconfidence a major turnoff in a partner."
  • General interest or enthusiasm — A turnoff can also describe something that discourages you from pursuing or enjoying anything, not just a person.
    • "The high price was a turnoff — I decided not to buy it."
    • "The aggressive sales tactics were a turnoff; I left without looking at anything."
  • Social or professional settings — Certain behaviors in public or at work can be called turnoffs too.
    • "Interrupting people constantly is a turnoff in a job interview."
The core idea behind both meanings

Both meanings share the same underlying image: something that causes you to deviate from your current path or direction — either physically (you leave the main road) or emotionally/mentally (you leave behind your interest or attraction).

In meaning 1, the turnoff is neutral — it is simply a road feature.
In meaning 2, the turnoff carries a negative charge — it is something unwelcome that pushes you away.

A turnoff can be mild or severe, depending on how strongly it repels you. Notice how speakers use intensifiers to signal this:

  • "It was a bit of a turnoff." (mild — it slightly reduced my enthusiasm)
  • "It was a real turnoff." (moderate — it genuinely bothered me)
  • "It was a massive/huge/instant turnoff." (strong — it completely killed my interest)

• It is not just something you dislike in passing. A turnoff specifically diminishes attraction, enthusiasm, or willingness to engage with something or someone.
  • It is not a permanent judgment. You might have one turnoff about a person but still like them overall. The word describes a reaction to a specific thing, not a total verdict.

Picture a light switch. Your interest, enthusiasm, or attraction is the light — it is on. A turnoff is the thing that flips that switch to off. The light goes out. That reaction — the moment the switch flips — is what the word captures.
16445: The word turnout has several distinct meanings. I'll walk you through each one clearly, with examples, so you understand exactly when and how each is used.
Meaning 1: The number of people who attend or participate in something

This is the most common and widely used meaning in modern English.

When someone says "turnout," they usually mean how many people showed up — to a vote, a protest, a concert, a match, a meeting, or any public event. It measures attendance or participation.

Examples:

  • "Voter turnout was very low in this election." → Fewer people than expected actually came out to vote.
  • "Despite heavy rain, there was a great turnout at the charity run." → Many people still showed up.
  • "The festival attracted a record turnout of 80,000 people." → 80,000 people attended.

Notice that turnout isn't just a raw number — it often carries a sense of how impressive or disappointing the attendance was. A "high turnout" is good; a "low turnout" is concerning.

You will very frequently see it paired with:

  • voter turnout — the proportion of eligible voters who actually voted
  • high/low turnout
  • strong/poor turnout
  • record turnout — more people than ever before
Meaning 2: A widened section of a narrow road

On narrow roads — especially rural or mountain roads — where two vehicles cannot pass each other side by side, builders construct occasional wider spots at intervals along the road. One vehicle can pull into this wider section and wait while the other passes. That wider section is called a turnout.

It is also used for a small area beside a main road where a driver can pull over temporarily — to check a map, take a photo, rest, or let emergency vehicles pass.

Examples:

  • "The mountain road was barely one lane wide, but every kilometer there was a turnout where cars could let each other pass."
  • "The driver pulled into a turnout and switched off the engine."

This meaning is especially common in American English and in contexts involving rural or scenic roads.
Meaning 3: A railway switch or junction

In railway terminology, a turnout is the mechanical arrangement of tracks that allows a train to move from one track onto another branching track. It is the point where one line diverges from another.

In British English, this same thing is often called "points"; in American English, it is called a "switch" or a "turnout."

Example:

  • "The train slowed as it approached the turnout to shift onto the branch line."
Meaning 4: A person's appearance, outfit, or a smart horse-drawn carriage (old-fashioned / literary)

In older or more formal English — the kind you find in 19th- and early 20th-century literature — turnout referred to the overall way a person was dressed and presented, their smartness of appearance. It could also refer to a complete horse-drawn carriage along with its horses, harness, and driver — the whole package as a visual display.

Examples:

  • "The general's turnout was flawless — uniform pressed, buttons gleaming, posture perfect." → His appearance and presentation were immaculate.
  • "The duchess arrived in an admirable turnout." → She arrived in a fine, well-equipped carriage with matched horses.

You will mostly encounter this meaning in classic literature or period dramas. It is rarely used in everyday modern speech, but knowing it will help you understand older texts.
Meaning 5: A thorough clearing-out or cleaning of a space (chiefly British English)

In British English, a turnout can mean the act of emptying a room, cupboard, drawer, or storage space — going through everything, sorting it out, throwing away what is no longer needed, and cleaning the space.

Examples:

  • "I gave the spare room a good turnout and donated three boxes of old books."
  • "The office is overdue for a turnout — there are files here from fifteen years ago."

You will hear this mostly in informal British speech.
Meaning 6: A workers' strike or walkout (historical)

In 19th-century British English — particularly in writing about the Industrial Revolution and factory labour — a turnout meant a strike, where workers collectively stopped working and "turned out" of the factory in protest to demand better pay or conditions.

Example:

  • "The mill workers organized a turnout to protest the wage cuts."

This meaning is now obsolete in everyday use, but you will come across it in historical texts, novels, and accounts from that era.
How to tell which meaning is intended

Since turnout carries several meanings, context always makes it clear:

  • Talking about an election, rally, concert, or gathering? → It means the number of people who attended.
  • Talking about a road? → It means a wider section where vehicles can pull over.
  • Talking about a railway? → It means a track switch or junction.
  • Talking about someone's appearance or a carriage? → It means their outfit/presentation or the whole vehicle.
  • Talking about cleaning a room or storage? → It means a clearout (British).
  • In a historical, industrial context about workers? → It means a strike.
A note on the word's feel

The word turnout always carries a sense of something coming outward or into view. People turn out (come out) for an event. A road turns out (broadens outward). A railway turns out (branches outward). A person's appearance is what they turn out to the world. Workers turn out of a factory. This shared sense of emerging or spreading outward is woven through every meaning.
16446: The word turnover captures one core idea: things cycling out and being replaced. Think of it like a wheel turning — something goes out, something new comes in. This core idea plays out in several different areas of life, and once you grasp it, all the meanings will make perfect sense.

This is the most common meaning you'll encounter in business and finance.

A company's turnover is the total amount of money it earns from selling its goods or services over a period of time — usually a year. It is not profit. It is the raw total that flows in from customers before any costs are subtracted.

"The supermarket chain reported a turnover of ₹500 crore last year."

This means the supermarket collected ₹500 crore from customers through sales. Whether they made a profit after paying for rent, staff, and supplies is a separate question.

Why is it called "turnover"? Because money keeps cycling — goods go out, money comes in, you buy more goods, sell them again. The stock turns over, and each cycle generates revenue. The total of all those cycles is your turnover.

Key distinction to remember:

  • Turnover = all the money coming in from sales (also called revenue or gross sales)
  • Profit = what's left after you subtract all your costs from the turnover

If a business has a high turnover but high costs, it can still make very little profit — or even a loss.
2. In Employment: Staff or Employee Turnover

Employee turnover refers to the rate at which workers leave a company and are replaced by new ones.

"The restaurant has a very high turnover — most waiters quit within three months."

Again, the core idea of cycling applies: employees come in, leave, and new ones take their place. When this happens frequently, we say turnover is high. When employees stay for a long time, turnover is low.

High turnover is generally seen as a problem for companies. It costs money and time to hire and train new people repeatedly. It also signals that something may be wrong — poor management, low pay, bad working conditions, or a stressful environment.

Low turnover usually means employees are satisfied and choose to stay.

You'll often see phrases like:

"The tech startup struggled with high turnover."
"The school's low staff turnover meant students had consistent teachers for years."

This meaning is closely related to the business meaning above, but it focuses on physical goods rather than money.

Stock (or inventory) turnover refers to how quickly a business sells and replenishes its products.

"The electronics store has a high turnover on smartphones — they sell out every model within weeks."

If a shop buys 100 units of a product and sells all 100 quickly before restocking, that product has a high turnover. If items sit on shelves for months, turnover is low.

A high stock turnover is generally good — it means products are selling fast and cash isn't stuck in unsold goods. A low turnover can mean the business has bought too much stock, the products aren't popular, or they're priced too high.

In many team sports — especially basketball and American football — a turnover means a moment when one team unintentionally loses the ball to the opposing team, without the period of play ending naturally.

"The team committed five turnovers in the second half and lost the game."

A turnover happens through:

  • A fumble (dropping the ball, in American football)
  • An interception (the other team catches a pass meant for your teammate)
  • Stepping out of bounds while holding the ball
  • Violating a rule that gives the other team possession

The idea is the same: control of the ball turns over from one team to the other, unexpectedly. Turnovers are costly because they give the opponent an opportunity to score.
5. In Food: A Type of Pastry

A turnover is a small, individual pastry made by placing a filling on one half of a flat piece of dough, then folding (turning over) the other half on top of it, sealing the edges, and baking or frying it.

"She had an apple turnover with her morning tea."

Common fillings include apple, cherry, cheese, or chocolate. The pastry is typically triangular or semicircular in shape.

The name is very literal: the dough is turned over onto the filling.
6. The General Sense: Rate of Replacement

Outside of these specific contexts, turnover can describe how quickly anything is replaced or cycled through in a general sense.

"There's a fast turnover of customers at this café — people come in, order quickly, and leave."
"The turnover of fashion trends has gotten faster with social media."

Wherever something moves through a cycle — in and out, in and out — you can describe the speed of that cycle as its turnover.

ContextWhat "turns over"
Business revenueMoney from sales cycles in
EmploymentEmployees cycle out and are replaced
Retail/InventoryProducts sell and are restocked
SportsBall possession switches sides
FoodDough is folded over filling
GeneralAnything cycles through repeatedly

The thread connecting every meaning is the same simple image: something cycling, replacing, or flipping over. Once that clicks, you'll recognize the word instantly in any context.
16447:
A turnpike is a road — specifically, a major road where you must pay a toll (a fee) in order to use it. The toll is collected at specific points along the road, called toll booths or toll plazas. You drive up, pay your fee (either to a person in a booth, or at an automated machine), and then you're allowed to continue on the road.

Think of it like a cinema — you don't get in without a ticket. A turnpike is a road you don't get to use without paying first.

Roads — especially large, well-maintained highways — are very expensive to build and to keep in good condition. Turnpikes are a way of saying: the people who actually use this road should pay for it. The money collected from tolls goes toward maintaining the road, repaying the cost of building it, and sometimes expanding it further.

This is different from an ordinary road or street, which is paid for through general government taxes — meaning everyone pays for it, whether they use it or not. A turnpike shifts that cost directly onto its users.

The word "turnpike" is used in two related senses:

1. The road itself — This is the dominant modern meaning. When people say "turnpike," they almost always mean the toll road as a whole. For example, "Take the turnpike north for about 50 miles" means: get on that toll highway and drive north.

2. The barrier/gate at the toll point — Historically, "turnpike" also referred to the physical gate or barrier placed across the road. You would pay the toll-keeper, and they would open (or rotate) the gate to let you through. This is the older, original meaning. Today, almost nobody uses "turnpike" to mean the gate itself — the word now refers to the road.

In 18th and 19th century Britain, turnpikes were extremely common. Groups called turnpike trusts were given legal authority to maintain specific stretches of road, collect tolls from travelers, and use that money for upkeep. Before this system, roads were often in terrible condition. Turnpike trusts transformed road travel by creating financial accountability — if you charge people to use a road, you have an obligation to keep it in good shape.

By the late 19th and early 20th century, as governments took over road maintenance more directly (and later as cars replaced horse-drawn travel), the turnpike trust system faded in Britain. The word "turnpike" is now mostly historical in British English.

In the United States today, "turnpike" is a living, commonly used word. It refers to major toll highways — often long, well-maintained expressways designed for fast, long-distance travel. These roads are typically part of the interstate or state highway system.

Some well-known American turnpikes:

  • New Jersey Turnpike — one of the busiest and most famous toll roads in the US, running through the heart of New Jersey
  • Pennsylvania Turnpike — stretching across Pennsylvania, one of the oldest toll highways in America
  • Ohio Turnpike — running across northern Ohio along the I-80 corridor
  • Massachusetts Turnpike — crossing Massachusetts east to west (locals often just call it "the Pike")
  • Florida's Turnpike — a major north-south highway in Florida

In casual American speech, people sometimes shorten "turnpike" to just "the pike" — as in, "Jump on the pike and you'll be there in an hour."
How is "turnpike" different from similar words?

These words are related but not interchangeable:

  • Road / highway — A broad term for any major road. No implication of tolls.
  • Freeway / expressway — A high-speed road with limited entry and exit points (ramps, not traffic lights). These may or may not have tolls.
  • Toll road — The general term for any road where you pay a toll. A turnpike is a type of toll road, but specifically one that is a large, significant highway.
  • Motorway (British English) — The British equivalent of a freeway or expressway. In the UK, motorways are generally free (paid for by taxes), so they are not turnpikes.
  • Turnpike — A major toll highway. The word carries a sense of significance and size; you wouldn't call a small local toll lane a turnpike.

In short: all turnpikes are toll roads, but not all toll roads are turnpikes. The word specifically suggests a major, long-distance highway.
How it's used in a sentence

• "The quickest route is the turnpike — it'll cost you a couple of dollars in tolls, but you'll save 40 minutes."
  • "Traffic on the turnpike is backed up for miles because of an accident near exit 12."
  • "She drove the entire length of the Pennsylvania Turnpike in one day."
  • "Before the turnpike was built, it took twice as long to cross the state."

A turnpike is a major road — typically a large highway — where drivers pay a toll (fee) to use it. The toll is collected at booths or plazas along the route. The concept originated in Britain as a system of privately managed toll roads, and while that historical usage has faded, the word is very much alive in American English, where it names some of the country's most important highways. A turnpike is simply a road with a price tag attached to using it.
16448: A turnstile is a mechanical gate that lets only one person pass through at a time. It is designed to control access — meaning it decides who gets in and how many people enter.

Picture a vertical metal post fixed firmly to the ground. Attached to this post, at about waist height, are three or four horizontal metal arms arranged like the spokes of a wheel (or like a plus sign + viewed from above). These arms stick out in different directions and can rotate in one direction around the post.

When you push one arm forward, the whole set of arms rotates, the arm in front of you moves away, and you can step through the gap it leaves. As soon as you pass, the next arm swings into place and blocks the path again — ready for the next person.

This is the most common and classic type, often called a waist-height turnstile or a three-arm turnstile.

A turnstile serves one or more of these jobs:

  1. Controls entry — It makes sure people enter in an orderly, single-file manner, one at a time.
  2. Restricts unauthorized access — In many places, the arms are locked by default. They only unlock after you do something — swipe a transit card, insert a coin or token, scan a ticket, or press a button. This ensures only people who have paid or have permission can enter.
  3. Counts people — Because each rotation lets exactly one person through, turnstiles are very reliable for counting how many people have entered a place.
  4. Prevents going backwards — Most turnstiles are built to rotate in only one direction. You can push through forward, but you cannot push back the other way. This stops people from sneaking in through the exit side.

Turnstiles are extremely common in everyday life:

  • Metro/subway and railway stations — The most familiar use. You tap your card or scan your ticket, the arm unlocks, you walk through. Without paying, the arm stays locked and blocks you.
  • Bus terminals and airports
  • Sports stadiums and concert venues — To check tickets before letting fans into the seating area.
  • Amusement parks and theme parks — To verify entry passes.
  • Office buildings and corporate campuses — For security; only authorized employees with ID cards can enter.
  • Museums, zoos, and exhibitions
  • Public toilets (in some countries) — Requiring a small coin payment.

Besides the common waist-height type, there is also a full-height turnstile (sometimes called a "full-height gate"). This version extends from floor to ceiling and looks like a revolving door made of metal bars rather than glass panels. It is used in places that need very high security — like prisons, construction sites, power plants, or high-security offices — because it is nearly impossible to jump over or crawl under.

In English, the word "turnstile" is sometimes used figuratively (not literally) to describe a situation where people or things pass through very rapidly and in large numbers, as if moving through a gate.

For example:

  • A hospital that sees an enormous number of patients every day might be described as a "turnstile hospital" — meaning patients come and go so quickly that the place feels like a transit gate, not a place of careful care.
  • A company where employees constantly quit and new ones are hired might be called a "turnstile workplace".
  • In sports commentary, "turnstile attendance" refers to the actual number of fans counted as they passed through the entry gates, as opposed to tickets sold.

The underlying idea in all these cases is the same: rapid, continuous, one-by-one movement through a point.

A turnstile is a rotating mechanical gate with arms, installed at an entrance, that lets only one person through at a time — usually after payment or authorization — while blocking, counting, and directing the flow of people.
16449:
Turpitude means deep, shameful wickedness. It refers to behavior that is so morally corrupt and so fundamentally wrong that it offends the basic values of decent society. Think of it not as ordinary bad behavior, but as the kind of moral rottenness that makes people feel genuine disgust and outrage.

If someone lies about being late to work, that's a flaw. If someone systematically deceives and robs elderly people out of their life savings while pretending to care for them — that is turpitude. The word lives at the extreme end of the moral scale.

Very strong. Turpitude is not used lightly. It implies a serious, deep-seated moral corruption — not a momentary lapse in judgment, not a bad habit, not a human imperfection. It suggests something rotten at the core. When you call someone's actions "turpitude," you are saying their behavior is not just wrong, but beneath the threshold of what any decent human being should do.
The phrase you'll almost always see it in

The word almost never appears alone in real-world usage. Instead, it nearly always appears in the phrase "moral turpitude." This phrase is especially important in legal language — particularly in immigration law, criminal law, and professional licensing.

In those contexts, "moral turpitude" is a formal, legal way of saying: this act is so contrary to accepted standards of honesty, justice, and good morals that it cannot be overlooked. Crimes that typically fall under this label include fraud, serious theft, sexual offenses, murder, and acts of deliberate cruelty. If an immigrant is convicted of a crime involving moral turpitude, it can be grounds for deportation. If a licensed professional — a doctor, a lawyer — commits an act of moral turpitude, they can lose their license. The phrase carries serious legal consequences.

This is important to understand, because the word's power comes partly from knowing where its boundary lies. Turpitude is not:

Everyday human weakness — forgetting a promise, losing your temper, making a poor decision under stress. These are imperfections, not turpitude.

Minor dishonesty — telling a small lie to avoid an awkward situation does not rise to this level.

Mistakes, even serious ones — turpitude implies deliberate moral wrongdoing, not accidents or errors in judgment.

Turpitude requires a certain quality of intentional wickedness, corruption, or depravity. It is about character at its worst, not circumstance at its worst.

Here are sentences that show how the word is naturally used:

"The senator's years of corruption and betrayal of public trust revealed a man of extraordinary turpitude."

"She was denied citizenship after a background check uncovered a prior conviction for a crime of moral turpitude."

"The commission concluded that the officer's conduct — planting evidence and lying under oath — constituted moral turpitude and warranted permanent dismissal."

"History has judged the actions of those leaders not as political failures, but as acts of outright turpitude."
The tone and register of the word

Turpitude is a formal, somewhat elevated word. You will find it most commonly in legal documents, court rulings, formal writing, literature, journalism dealing with serious ethical scandals, and serious moral or philosophical discussions. You would not use it in casual everyday conversation — it would sound out of place. But in formal writing or speech, when you want to communicate the gravity of someone's moral failure with precision and weight, turpitude is exactly the right word.

Turpitude = deep, deliberate moral corruption and wickedness — the kind that violates what society considers the most basic standards of decent human behavior. It is serious, it is intentional, and it sits at the far end of what is morally acceptable. Its most important and common form is the legal phrase "moral turpitude," which carries real consequences in courts, immigration proceedings, and professional licensing.
